1.d4 f5 2.e4.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.e4.background: Named after Howard Staunton, who played it against Bernhard Horwitz in London in 1846. Once a feared weapon for White, it is rarely played today, since defensive techniques have been developed to neutralise it.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit Accepted
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn: Black wins material, and White must prove compensation with fast development and attacking chances against a kingside loosened by the f-pawn's departure. Black has to defend accurately and be ready to give the pawn back.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 d6.strategy: Declines the gambit without winning anything: White gets the centre and the pieces come out with tempo, whether the pawns trade on e4 or on f5. The c8 bishop is freed, but the weak diagonal to the king stays a target, and White is simply better.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 e6.strategy: Guards f5 and frees the king's bishop, but 3.exf5 exf5 gives White the bigger centre and an open e-file with the king still in the middle. The weak diagonal to the king stays a target, so declining costs more than accepting.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3.strategy: The natural answer: the knight attacks the e4 pawn at once and develops towards the centre, so Black has to defend it or give it back. White is in no hurry, because the pawn was given for quick development and a weakened diagonal in front of Black's king.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nd2.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit, American Attack
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nd2.strategy: Goes after the pawn with the other knight, which also attacks e4 and leaves the c-pawn free. But it boxes in the c1 bishop, and Black can simply defend the pawn with a developing move, so the gambit loses much of its bite.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop before the knight and leaves the e4 pawn unattacked for now, so Black has time to consolidate the extra pawn. Against natural development White reaches the main line anyway; otherwise the early bishop commits White to the gambit without winning anything back yet.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn and develops a piece in one move. The knight also covers h5, which takes away the queen's check on the weakened diagonal for now. Black keeps the extra pawn and waits to see how White means to win it back.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and eyes d4, but leaves the e4 pawn undefended: d5 drives the knight off with tempo and Nxe4 then regains the pawn. Black returns the gambit pawn and falls behind in the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Takes h5 away from the queen, so the check on the weakened diagonal disappears, and prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to guard the weakened kingside. It leaves e4 undefended, though: White takes the pawn back with Nxe4 and material is level.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.background: The main line of the gambit. Staunton first played 4.Bg5 in the London game against Horwitz in 1846.
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: The main line: the bishop attacks the knight that defends e4, threatening to take it and win the pawn back with Black's structure damaged. It also keeps the queen's check on h5 in reserve for when the knight goes. Black has to answer the threat precisely.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3.name: Dutch Defence: Blackmar's Second Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3.strategy: Offers a second pawn to open the centre and bring the pieces out with tempo. Taking it with ...exf3 gives White real compensation, so Black does better to strike back in the centre at once and keep the extra material.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit, Tartakower Variation
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g4.strategy: Throws the g-pawn forward to drive the knight from f6, loosening White's own king while a pawn down. Black answers with the quiet ...h6, yet the open lines still give White real play, so it is playable, though riskier than the main move.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit, Chigorin Variation
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6.strategy: Prepares the central strike ...d5 with a pawn behind it: played at once, that strike would run into a tactic on the weakened kingside, while with the c-pawn in support it works. Black accepts that White may regain the pawn and plays for a solid game.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 g6.strategy: Shuts the h5-e8 diagonal for good and prepares to fianchetto the bishop, so the king gets the safety the gambit was aimed at. The cost is the h6 square, which the g5 bishop already attacks, and the e4 pawn is still hard to hold.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 b6.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit, Nimzowitsch Variation
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 as a second defender of the e4 pawn, so Black tries to keep the extra pawn instead of returning it. The cost is time: Black spends a move on the queenside while the g5 bishop presses on f6 and the king's side stays open.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 g6 5.h.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit, Alekhine Variation
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 g6 5.h.strategy: Supports the bishop on g5, which makes ...h6 a poor way to drive it back, and prepares h5 to attack the g6 pawn. White plays for a direct attack on Black's kingside instead of simply winning the pawn back.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 g6 5.f.name: Dutch Defence: Staunton Gambit, Lasker Variation
1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 g6 5.f.strategy: Opens the centre and the f-file at once: after ...exf3 the knight recaptures with a developing move and White's pieces come out quickly. But White is still a pawn down, and Black's kingside is sound behind the fianchetto.

1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 g6 5.B.strategy: Takes the knight at once. With the g-pawn on g6 the bishop on f6 also attacks the h8 rook, so Black has to retake with the e-pawn, and Nxe4 then wins the gambit pawn back. White settles for a level game; Black keeps the bishop pair but a clumsy pawn mass on f6, g6 and h7.
